searchText: SSZ is already very similar to the ABI (the serialization I mean) In fact I think the main differences are (i) 4 bytes for length instead of 32, (ii) little instead of big endian Ok, after the ACD call on friday, I went and did that analysis of whether EIP-2930 is needed. https://github.com/holiman/eip2929-stats . TLDR: Yes, roughly 1K out of 650K transactions are bottle-necked by a `2300` send cc <@!364458974906548225> <@!273808422753796097> ^ <@273808422753796097> Is it correct that there is no fundamental benefit in SSZ over RLP (other than some beauty and simplicity) if merklization is not enabled? I believe this is true, yes. It is the SSZ Merklization that brings most of the benefits. There are some nice-to-haves in SSZ over RLP, but a lot of that stuff is debatable and not obvious big wins. Things like fixed width structures being able to have data plucked is "nice". Just wanted a second confirmation 🙂 Piper would probably be a good person to comment on that then. Can you explain what you mean my "merklization not enabled"? I've got an impression during the call that introduction of SSZ would only imply serialization to bytes, and not computation of a canonical hash of the structure as the merkle tree (so instead just hash of the serialized data would be used) <@!364458974906548225> I believe they mean use SSZ serialization, but then hash the object like `keccak256(ssh(struct, description))` The idea being that SSZ serialization is "simple" while SSZ merklization is "complicated", so there is lower risk introducing only SSZ serialization. SSZ would still be an improvement to RLP for serialization but not necessarily a big enough improvement to justify the cost of transition. I think there's a broader benefit that still hasn't been captured. Since SSZ gives us schemas, serialization, merklization and hashing, it is useful to think of it as a building block for simplifying the overall protocol. These are common "tools" that are regularly needed when trying to specify parts of the protocol. If we use SSZ, we can lean on a common toolbox for specifying the protocols which should make our specifications simpler since they can use an SSZ schema for defining the data structures involved and automatically get well defined serializations, merklization, and hashing for free (without having to explicitely define how to do each of these things). Is there any consensus on how serving the light clients will work and be incentivized in eth2.0? In such case SSZ can be a huge benefit SSZ should be a huge benefit for light clients because of the native support for proofs and partial data retrieval. But for this you must ensure that such proofs are served for them, so I’m curious if there is some solution to incentivize it All I'm asserting is that SSZ provides more powerful building blocks to build light protocols on top of. Nobody has yet solved the "make a light client that just works" problem yet. Really hopped for the best
